citation.title: VoroTO: Multiscale Topology Optimization of Voronoi Structures using Surrogate Neural Networks
citation.authors: Rahul Kumar Padhy, Krishnan Suresh, Aaditya Chandrasekhar
citation.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.CE; also math.NA), CC BY 4.0; comment 'Submitted to Engineering with Computers'. Version of record: Engineering with Computers 41(2):1123-1139, doi 10.1007/s00366-024-02077-w, online 2024-10-29 (Crossref, OpenAlex); closed access per OpenAlex, and Crossref lists only Springer TDM licences; not read. Crossref also links a Research Square preprint (doi 10.21203/rs.3.rs-4339435/v1), which is not in the pool
citation.version_coded: arXiv v1 (28 Apr 2024; the only version), PDF (15 pages including references) read in full as text; the closed version of record was not read, so differences from it are unknown

included.reason: I-SPEED (screening code confirmed at full text; primary outcome chosen by §5.1 rules 2 and 4)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: For the 40x20 mid-cantilever, NN-surrogate multiscale Voronoi TO takes 0.24 min after a one-time 28.4 min (data plus training), versus a projected 528 min for concurrent homogenization-based multiscale TO and 4,986 min for brute-force fine-scale TO.
claim.key_phrase: the proposed offline NN-based multiscale optimization is computationally far superior
claim.location: Sec. 3.3 ('Is Offline Computation Justified?', pp. 10-11). The abstract and conclusion state the advantage over concurrent homogenization only qualitatively, and the introduction has no classical comparison. The main text's first classical comparisons are compliance values (Sec. 3.2.1-3.2.2); rule 4 takes Sec. 3.3, the comparison the conclusion emphasises
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Derived, not stated: projected concurrent-homogenization time 528 min / VoroTO optimization 0.24 min = 2,200 per run, excluding the one-time 28.4 min. Including the one-time cost for a single use: 528 / 28.64 = 18.4 [derived]. Against the brute-force projection: 4,986 / 0.24 = 20,775, or 174 including the one-time cost [derived]. Both classical times are projections from unit costs (0.132 s per homogenization; one measured 16.62 min iteration), each multiplied by 300 assumed iterations.
claim.alternatives: (1) Sec. 3.2.1 (first main-text compliance comparison): tensile bar, porous design 209 vs 183 for the single-scale design reported in [89] (an NN-based study; how that design was computed is not stated here). (2) Sec. 3.2.2: mid-cantilever at v = 0.6, VoroTO compliance 68.3 as predicted (74.6 at volume 0.65 on FE re-analysis) vs 61.05 for the single-scale 88-line code [95] and 76.86 for the infill design of [96]; computed in 13.7 s. (3) Conclusion, qualitative: significant computational advantages over concurrent homogenization with minimal loss in accuracy.

baseline.classical_method: Speed comparators: concurrent homogenization-based multiscale TO (numerical homogenization of every macro element at every iteration) and brute-force single-scale TO at the fine scale; both are projections, not runs (Sec. 3.3). Quality comparators: single-scale designs from the 88-line code [95] and from [89], and the infill optimization of [96] (Sec. 3.2.1-3.2.2)
baseline.implementation: The projections use the authors' own homogenization code (unit cost taken from the data-generation run) and an unstated single-scale code for the one timed 1600 x 800 iteration; VoroTO itself is in PyTorch (Sec. 2.5.3)
baseline.hardware_classical: MacBook M2 Air, 16 GB RAM (all experiments; Sec. 3)
baseline.hardware_ml: MacBook M2 Air, 16 GB RAM (all experiments; Sec. 3); CPU or GPU use not stated
baseline.problem_size: Macro mesh 40 x 20 elements with 4 Voronoi sites per element; homogenization mesh 120 x 120 per microstructure (Sec. 2.4.2); brute-force projection at 1600 x 800 elements (40 x 40 micro-elements per macro element; about 2.56 million DOFs [derived])
baseline.classical_iterations: 300 assumed in both projections, equal to VoroTO's iteration cap (Sec. 3, Sec. 3.3)
baseline.classical_time: Projected: 528 min for concurrent homogenization (0.132 s per homogenization x 800 elements x 300 iterations) and 4,986 min for brute force (one measured 16.62 min iteration x 300) (Sec. 3.3)
baseline.ml_time: 0.24 min per mid-cantilever optimization (Sec. 3.3); 13.7 s in Sec. 3.2.2 and the parameter studies (0.24 min = 14.4 s [derived])
baseline.data_generation_cost: 26.4 min for 12,000 homogenized microstructures (Sec. 3.3; data set in Sec. 3.1.1)
baseline.quality_metric: NN-predicted compliance and volume during optimization; for the mid-cantilever and heel-bone cases, microstructures rebuilt and re-homogenized by FEA, followed by macroscale FEA (Sec. 3.2.2, Sec. 3.2.4); compliance compared with single-scale and infill designs
baseline.quality_gap: Mid-cantilever: predicted compliance 68.3 vs 74.6 on re-analysis (8.4% error); volume 0.65 vs target 0.6 (stated error 6.1%; 8.3% relative to the target [derived]) (Sec. 3.2.2). Heel bone: errors below 10% (Sec. 3.2.4). No design exists from either projected classical method

R1.evidence: Sec. 3.3 (pp. 10-11): VoroTO's 0.24 min (plus the one-time 28.4 min) is set against projected times for concurrent homogenization (528 min) and brute-force fine-scale TO (4,986 min). Neither classical scenario was run, so no classical design exists at the timed budget. Quality is still reported for the same mid-cantilever: the VoroTO design (compliance 68.3 as predicted; 74.6 at volume 0.65 against the 0.6 target on FE re-analysis) is set against the classical single-scale 88-line design (61.05) and the infill design of [96] (76.86) (Sec. 3.2.2, pp. 8-9), and the claim is paired with a surrogate error below 10% against exact homogenization (Sec. 3.3, p. 11). Matching is loose: the volume is not matched, and the projections assume 300 iterations with no quality target. Neither fail marker is established: a quality comparison exists, and the projected classical runs have no output that could be shown better.

R2.evidence: Sec. 3.3: both classical times are projections. The concurrent-homogenization estimate assumes serial homogenization of all 800 elements at each of 300 iterations on a laptop, with no parallel or reuse strategy. The brute-force estimate multiplies one 16.62 min iteration at 1600 x 800 (about 2.56 million DOFs [derived]) by 300, with the solver not stated; that per-iteration time looks slow for the size [inferred] and is an input for an R2(e) re-test. (b) and (c) do not apply (one laptop for all runs). (d) is not established: 300 is VoroTO's own iteration cap, and the article gives no classical convergence data.

R3.evidence: Sec. 3.3: data generation (26.4 min) and training (2 min) are reported and set, with the 0.24 min run, against one projected classical run. The total, 28.64 min [derived], is below either projection, so the method breaks even at the first use.

R4.evidence: Sec. 3.2.2 and 3.2.4: for the mid-cantilever and heel-bone designs, the microstructures were rebuilt and re-analysed by homogenization FEA and macroscale FEA, and the re-analysed volume is reported (0.65 vs target 0.6). Figs. 14 and 17-19 report optimizer-side compliance values [inferred: NN-predicted]. Disconnected or failed microstructure layouts are not counted; filtering promotes connectivity, but connectivity is not measured.

reporting.n_test_cases: 11 distinct optimization runs [derived: tensile bar 1; mid-cantilever at v = 0.6, 1; six parameter-variation runs at v = 0.5 (Figs. 17-19, default run shared); heel bone 3 (Fig. 20)]; the timing comparison covers the mid-cantilever only (Sec. 3.3)

notes: Screening code was I-SPEED. Version: the Engineering with Computers version of record is closed (OpenAlex: closed; Crossref: Springer TDM licences only), so under the FT-DUPLICATE rule the latest arXiv version (v1, the only one) is the primary version; no other version is in the pool (title and 'Voronoi' searched). Primary-outcome judgment: abstract, introduction and conclusion hold no quantitative classical comparison. The main text holds compliance comparisons (Sec. 3.2.1-3.2.2) and the time comparison (Sec. 3.3). Rule 4 takes Sec. 3.3, because the conclusion's only classical claim is the computational advantage over concurrent homogenization. A strict 'first main-text comparison' reading would take the Sec. 3.2.1 tensile-bar compliance and give stratum Q. This batch applies the same rule-2-then-rule-4 reading to P00161 and P01219. Timing protocol: hardware stated (MacBook M2 Air); the classical times are projections from one measured iteration and a derived homogenization cost; no warm-up or repeats; hence partial. Runtimes: 13.7 s is given for the mid-cantilever runs, none for the tensile bar or heel bone, hence selective. Code: github.com/UW-ERSL/VoroTO (GitHub API, 2026-09-24: public, MIT licence, Python modules and notebooks for data generation, training and TO; the data folder holds no data files). retest_candidate true: public code under MIT and a runnable mid-cantilever benchmark. The classical side is a projection, which a re-test can check with the repository's homogenization code and our strong baseline (the 16.62 min iteration at 1600 x 800 for R2(e)). Minor inconsistencies: 0.24 min (Sec. 3.3) vs 13.7 s (Sec. 3.2.2); stated volume error 6.1% vs 8.3% for 0.65 against 0.6 [derived]. Authors checked: no author named Jun Wang (reference [96] is by Jun Wu, not a queue author). Adjudicator check (2026-09-24): the arXiv v1 PDF was re-read in full; the abs page lists v1 only. The agreed speed stratum is kept under §5.1 rule 4: the main text holds a quality comparison (Sec. 3.2.2, pp. 8-9) before the speed comparison (Sec. 3.3), and the conclusion (Sec. 4, p. 11) singles out the computational advantage over concurrent homogenization. Fig. 14's caption labels the [89] design 'multiscale', while the text calls it single-scale (Sec. 3.2.1, p. 8), so it is unclear whether [89]'s value comes from a classical method.

R1.reason: The timed classical scenarios are projections with no design (Sec. 3.3, pp. 10-11), but the same mid-cantilever design is compared on quality with the classical 88-line and infill designs (61.05 and 76.86 vs 68.3 predicted, 74.6 on FE re-analysis at volume 0.65; Sec. 3.2.2, pp. 8-9). So the 'no quality comparison' fail marker is not met (as in P00140), and the unmatched volume and assumed 300 iterations are the §5.3 R1 partial case.

R2.reason: The brute-force projection rests on one iteration of 16.62 min at 1600 x 800 elements (about 2.56 million DOFs [derived]) on a laptop, with code and solver unstated (Sec. 3.3, p. 10). That time is far above what the authors' own homogenization cost (0.132 s at 120 x 120) implies even with superlinear scaling [inferred], so the implementation looks inefficient, but only an R2(e) re-test can compare it. The 88-line code that the second coder cites is named only for the Sec. 3.2.2 quality design; the code of the timed iteration is not stated.

R4.reason: The mid-cantilever and heel-bone designs are FE re-analysed (Sec. 3.2.2, p. 9; Sec. 3.2.4, p. 10), but the 0.65 volume against the 0.6 bound is presented as a 6.1% error rather than as a violation, the heel-bone volumes appear only as errors below 10%, the tensile-bar and parameter-study compliances are not stated as FE-verified (Figs. 14, 17-19), and connectivity failures are not counted: the §5.3 R4 partial case.

claimed_speedup.reason: No factor is stated. The per-run ratio against the concurrent-homogenization projection, 528 / 0.24 = 2,200 (Sec. 3.3, pp. 10-11) [derived], uses the comparator the conclusion names (Sec. 4, p. 11) and is the lower of the two per-run ratios; the project keeps data and training costs out of the factor (as in P00176 and P00183) and handles them under R3. The second coder's 174.1 divides the brute-force projection by the one-time plus per-run time, which stays in the basis as an alternative.
